title: Revenue up 38%, and nothing sold more

data.workspace: region_revenue.sql, the monthly revenue by region, Harrow Outdoor Supply (fictional)

flags.label: Finance controller, Abby Lin
flags.text: Your report says October revenue was 1.38 million. The ledger says 1.00 million. The board pack locks at 17:00.

flags.label: Pattern
flags.text: The gap appeared when shipments were added to the query for the region column.

lines.text: FROM orders o JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = o.order_id
WITH r AS (SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id) order_id, region FROM shipments ORDER BY order_id, shipped_at)
SELECT r.region, sum(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN r ON r.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY r.region;
SELECT s.region, sum(DISTINCT o.total) FROM orders o JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY s.region;
SELECT s.region, sum(o.total) / count(*) * count(DISTINCT o.order_id) FROM orders o JOIN shipments s USING (order_id) GROUP BY s.region;

objective: Recognize row multiplication when joining to a many-side table and correct the totals it inflates
secondaryObjectives: Write inner joins on key columns with table aliases and qualified column names

sources.cite: Looker Community, The problem of SQL fanouts
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. A one-to-many join 'can result in a fanout, and aggregate functions are not necessarily accurate'; check by comparing COUNT(*) before and after the join; pre-aggregate the many side by the join key so each primary row matches once.

brief.situation: You maintain region_revenue.sql at Harrow Outdoor Supply (fictional). Last month a join to shipments was added to get each order's region. Since then October revenue reads 1.38 million against a ledger total of 1.00 million. Orders that ship in several boxes have several shipment rows. The board pack locks at 17:00. It is 16:05.
handover: orders: one row per order with total. shipments: one row per box, with region.

Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Shipping is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

scoring.modelReasoning: The jump started when shipments joined in, and orders to shipments is one-to-many. Counting rows before and after the join shows 8,420 becoming 11,610: multi-box orders are repeated, and sum counts them repeatedly. Reduce shipments to one region per order in a CTE, then join and sum. sum(DISTINCT) drops different orders with equal totals; scaling by a ratio is wrong per region. Reconcile to the ledger.
